🇲🇽💻 <u>Public-university grads build 279 government apps and save 14 billion pesos</u>

The Agency for Digital Transformation (ATDT) says its in-house Software Factory, made up of 300 young graduates of public universities, has built 279 digital products. Building them in-house instead of hiring private contractors has saved the government more than 14 billion pesos.

Its new AI Factory is now developing tools for customs, invoice-fraud detection, patent assignment at IMPI and 24/7 citizen service. Under José Antonio Peña Merino, the state is building its own technology instead of renting it from consultancies.

🇲🇽⚖️ <u>Born abroad to Mexican parents? You're Mexican by birth, and can run for governor</u>

Presidential legal counsel Luisa María Alcalde clarified that under Article 30 of the Constitution, anyone born abroad to a Mexican mother or father is Mexican by birth, and so meets Article 116's requirement to run for governor. "A person may have been born on foreign soil but has Mexican parents," she said.

The question came up over Morena's Nayarit coordinator, Senator Jasmine Bugarín. The SRE confirmed she gave up her dual nationality in 2018, before the new constitutional reform barring dual nationals from the presidency and governorships. That reform has now been ratified by 20 state congresses, and it won't apply immediately.

🇲🇽🌊 <u>Cleanup of Mexico's three dirtiest rivers is 82% done</u>

Conagua director Efraín Morales reports that the first stage of the 20-billion-peso cleanup of the Atoyac, Lerma-Santiago and Tula rivers is 82% complete. So far that means 23 treatment plants built or rehabilitated, 282 km of sewage collectors, 260 km of riverbeds cleared, 4,663 hectares reforested and 44 water-quality monitoring stations.

Enforcement is moving too. In September Profepa shut down four illegal discharge points on tributaries of the Atoyac in Puebla, and Conagua filed a criminal complaint with the FGR after a municipal truck in El Salto, Jalisco, was filmed dumping sludge into a channel that feeds the Santiago.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>US hands Mexico 20 more fugitives, bringing the total to 370</u>

US Ambassador Ronald Johnson announced that 20 more fugitives wanted in Mexico have been handed over to Mexican authorities, on charges including homicide, kidnapping, money laundering and drug trafficking. That brings the total to more than 370 since January 2025.

It's the other side of the security deal Sheinbaum keeps defending: cooperation, not subordination. Mexico has sent dozens of cartel figures north, and now the people who fled to the US are coming back to face Mexican courts.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Fuel-theft investigations jump 40.56% as the FGR goes after huachicol</u>

INEGI's new federal justice census shows that cases the Fiscalía General de la República (FGR) opened for hydrocarbon crimes rose from 6,807 in 2024 to 9,568 in 2025, a 40.56% increase. Only crimes involving weapons and explosives were more common in the FGR's caseload.

Overall, crimes the FGR registered went up 7% to 84,144, while state prosecutors recorded 4.9% fewer. The jump comes from a federal crackdown on fuel theft, including huachicol fiscal: fuel smuggled into Mexico on fake customs paperwork.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>T-MEC talks: Mexico close to cutting US auto tariffs from 25% to 15%</u>

According to El Financiero, Mexican officials say the two governments are working out a deal that would cut the US tariff on Mexican light vehicles from 25% to 15%. Because the tariff only applies to non-US content, the effective rate would be 10–12%. The 50% tariffs on steel and aluminum are also on the table.

Mexico is still pushing for better terms than the 15% nominal rate Canada was offered last month. Ebrard says Mexico has handed Washington studies justifying preferential treatment. About 800,000 Mexicans work in the auto industry.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Fake "government" billboards attack the Mexico–Querétaro train</u>

Billboards across Querétaro blame traffic jams on the Mexico City–Querétaro passenger train, and they use the federal government's official logo, typography, maroon-and-white colors and seals. Santiago Nieto, who coordinates the Committees for the Defense of the Transformation and National Sovereignty in Querétaro, has taken the case to IMPI, the industrial property institute.

Nieto calls it an intellectual-property violation meant to confuse the public and run a disinformation campaign against a federal public works project. He is demanding that whoever paid for the billboards be identified and sanctioned.

🇲🇽🌽 <u>Mexico City aims to double its corn harvest, GMO-free</u>

For National Corn Day, Clara Brugada set a goal of doubling Mexico City's corn output, which now stands at 8,000 tons a year on more than 4,000 hectares. Her 10-point plan includes the Altépetl program, which gives more than 1 billion pesos a year to almost 2,500 growers, and a decree that declares the capital free of transgenic corn.

Federal Agriculture Secretary Columba López said corn supply is guaranteed until at least 2030, so tortilla prices won't rise. Mexicans eat 130.7 kg of corn per person each year, more than anyone else on Earth, and the grain was born here.

🇲🇽🧬 <u>First fully Mexican-made CAR-T cancer therapy goes to clinical trial</u>

Cofepris approved Mexico's first clinical trial of CAR-T cells manufactured entirely in the country. The UANL University Hospital in Monterrey will run protocol 7192 for adults with relapsed or treatment-resistant acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

Every step happens in Mexico: drawing the patient's T-cells, modifying them genetically, quality control and treatment, "without depending on the drug being manufactured or modified in another country." CAR-T treatments cost hundreds of thousands of dollars per patient abroad.

🇲🇽🌎 <u>Mexico's ambassador walks into ICE detention centers</u>

Roberto Lazzeri, Mexico's ambassador to the US, went into Prairieland and Montgomery in Texas and Caroline in Virginia to check on Mexicans held by ICE. He also met ICE officials in Dallas, Houston and Atlanta to press for consular protection and dignified treatment.

The visit came as reports surfaced that 79 detainees in a Florida facility were locked in metal cages. Marking his first 100 days on the job, Lazzeri called the detention of Mexican migrants "the greatest tragedy" he has seen, and said defending the community is Sheinbaum's direct order.
